<div class="clt-lesson batch-lesson" data-lesson="review"><h2 id="learning-goals">What are we trying to understand?</h2><p><strong>How can we turn statistical results into accurate, useful research conclusions?</strong></p><p>The final resource brings the course together through reporting exercises and cumulative knowledge checks. It is not a graded assessment; it is a practice space for revising explanations and identifying misconceptions.</p><div class="clt-overview"><strong>Learning goals</strong><ol><li>Communicate estimates, uncertainty and statistical evidence in context.</li><li>Separate statistical significance, practical importance and causality.</li><li>Identify design and assumption limitations.</li><li>Review major concepts across the entire learning pathway.</li></ol></div><h2 id="explore">Make a prediction and explore</h2><section class="clt-simulator"><h3>Interpretation workshop</h3><p>A hypothetical independent-groups study reports a mean difference of +4.2 attention-score points (workshop minus comparison), 95% CI [0.8, 7.6], p = .018 using Welch’s t-test. Participation was voluntary. No minimum practically meaningful difference was specified.</p><label for="draft"><strong>Draft a two- or three-sentence research conclusion:</strong></label><textarea id="draft" placeholder="Describe the estimated difference, uncertainty, evidence and limits."></textarea><p class="note">Your draft is not saved or transmitted. Copy it if you wish to keep it.</p><details><summary>Compare with a model interpretation</summary><p>Workshop participants averaged an estimated 4.2 points higher than the comparison group (95% CI 0.8 to 7.6; p = .018). Under the test assumptions, the data provide evidence of a difference in population means, but voluntary participation limits causal interpretation. Practical importance remains unclear without a substantive benchmark.</p></details><h3>Practice across the course</h3><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question data-correct="0" data-why="Large samples from a restricted frame can be precise but biased."><legend>A morning-only sample of 200 students estimates 42; the population mean is 50. Explain why statistical significance alone is insufficient.</li><li>Write a conclusion for a nonsignificant result with a wide interval. Explain the remaining uncertainty.</li><li>For your project, identify one limitation of sampling and one limitation of the analysis.</li><li>Review the questions you missed and return to the corresponding interactive lesson.</li></ol><h2 id="explanation">What is the method telling us?</h2><p>A useful statistical report answers the research question, describes the magnitude and direction of the estimate, quantifies uncertainty, and specifies what the evidence does and does not support. Use the language appropriate to the design: observational results indicate association unless additional causal assumptions and evidence justify a stronger claim.</p><div class="formula"><strong>Reporting checklist:</strong> Research question and population; design and sample; descriptive evidence; method and assumptions; estimate and interval; p-value and effect size where appropriate; practical meaning; limitations.</div><p>There is no single required narrative voice. The model language is a starting point for revising explanations to match your research context, audience and instructor expectations.</p><h2 id="knowledge-check">Check your understanding</h2><p>Choose an answer, then check your reasoning. Responses stay in your browser.</p><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question data-correct="1" data-why="An omnibus test does not identify specific group differences or practical importance."><legend>A one-way ANOVA p-value of .01 indicates what, under its assumptions?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="q0" value="0"> Every group differs from every other</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="q0" value="1"> Evidence at least one population mean differs</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="q0" value="2"> The largest mean is practically important</label><button class="clt-btn clt-secondary" type="button">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question data-correct="0" data-why="A significant result provides evidence against independence."><legend>A chi-square independence test is significant. Which statement is appropriate?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="q1" value="0"> Evidence of an association, not necessarily causation</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="q1" value="1"> Proof the workshop causes improvement</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="q1" value="2"> The variables are independent</label><button class="clt-btn clt-secondary" type="button">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question data-correct="1" data-why="Correlation does not establish a causal direction."><legend>Pearson r = .80 between study hours and test scores. What can be concluded?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="q2" value="0"> Study time causes higher scores</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="q2" value="1"> A strong positive linear association in the sample</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="q2" value="2"> 80% of students improved</label><button class="clt-btn clt-secondary" type="button">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question data-correct="1" data-why="Predictions outside the observed predictor range require caution."><legend>The regression slope is 2.5 points/hour, but predictions are made at 14 hours when observed times are 1–10.
